paragraphs.text: Automated review verified an artificial intelligence reference in 131 of 191 obtained 2026 General Debate addresses (68.6%), with 45 addresses still unresolved. This is a verified minimum, not an estimate of prevalence: unreviewed addresses are unknown, not negative. The verified minimum rose from 2 of 193 addresses in 2017 to 43 of 189 in 2023, 58 of 190 in 2024 and 74 of 189 in 2025. The 2025 and 2026 sources are unverified automatic transcripts rather than official English records, and 2026 has fewer unresolved addresses (45 against 97 in 2025), so part of the rise may reflect source type and review depth.

Verified minimums were highest among Western European and other States (24 of 28, 85.7%, none unresolved) and Eastern European States (17 of 23, 73.9%). Latin American and Caribbean States followed with 23 of 33 (69.7%), Asia-Pacific States with 33 of 52 (63.5%) and African States with 33 of 54 (61.1%). The lower African and Asia-Pacific figures coincide with more unresolved addresses (18 and 16), so regional gaps partly reflect review coverage rather than confirmed silence.

Method: automated full-speech review, a second review of an identified sample and two classification passes; there was no human verification. Theme shares use code-specific denominators, namely AI-positive 2026 addresses with a resolved value for that code, so denominators differ across themes and several addresses remain partly coded.

International rules and governance was the most frequent theme, verified in 65 of 105 resolved AI-positive addresses (61.9%); among 41 countries resolved in both years it rose from 18 to 23. Proposals ranged from Germany's call for common safety requirements, under which providers would “test these models before release and report serious safety failures”, to Bahrain's renewed call for “a binding international framework” and Singapore's appeal to “establish common rules and safeguards for AI”. Governance and the UN role were closely linked: of 37 addresses coded for a UN role, 32 also raised international governance.

The digital divide was raised in 50 of 114 resolved addresses (43.9%), development applications in 32 of 112 and capacity building in 27 of 119. The themes cluster: 20 of 23 addresses coded for capacity building also raised the divide. The Democratic Republic of the Congo warned that the “digital divide must not become an intelligence divide”, Bangladesh made a similar point, and Malawi cited unequal access to computing, data, skills and financing. Egypt asked that Arab and African languages be fairly represented in data and models, and the Bahamas sought AI that understands small states' languages.

Human rights and ethics appeared in 37 of 109 resolved addresses (33.9%) and explicit human control in 16 of 111. Both grew among matched countries: human rights from 6 to 16 of 40, human control from 0 to 7 of 51. Barbados asked for rules that “protect human dignity” and “preserve meaningful human oversight”, and Norway said AI “must remain under human direction, oversight, and control”. Egypt listed privacy, transparency, accountability and non-discrimination as governance principles. Bias and cultural diversity remained a minority theme (5 of 126).

Security risks were raised by fewer countries. Military AI and autonomous weapons appeared in 13 of 119 resolved addresses (10.9%), safety and catastrophic risk in 12 of 118, cybersecurity in 10 of 115 and disinformation in 8 of 120. Austria backed a legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons, stating “No machine may decide to take a human life”, and Slovakia said machines should never make life-or-death decisions on their own. Trinidad and Tobago listed deepfakes, autonomous weapons and threats to critical infrastructure. Military concerns fall outside the Panel and Dialogue, whose activities are limited to the non-military domain.

Concentration of power was raised in 26 of 112 resolved addresses (23.2%) and inclusive rule-making in 23 of 121 (19.0%). Germany noted that “Only two major countries are home to the companies holding the vast majority of all global AI patents”, Brazil criticised “technical oligarchs”, and Malaysia rejected rules set by a small number of companies or countries. Barbados argued that a technology affecting every state “must be governed by the rules that every state has had the opportunity to shape”. Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Malaysia linked AI to demand for minerals, energy or water (3 of 122).

A small but consequential minority questioned regulation or global approaches: scepticism was verified in 4 of 129 resolved addresses (Albania, Argentina, Nigeria, the United States). The United States “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” AI and described itself as leading China in a race; Argentina cited “a commitment not to regulate preemptively”; Albania warned “We cannot regulate ourselves into helplessness” while calling for a compact among democracies. Geopolitical rivalry appeared in 8 of 122 addresses, and three countries (Colombia, Trinidad and Tobago, the United States) used the term superintelligence.

A UN role in AI was verified in 45 of 120 resolved addresses (37.5%); among 55 matched countries it was stable (21 in 2025, 20 in 2026). Singapore called the UN “the only apex international institution with universal membership” and proposed exploring “a UN framework convention on AI safeguards”. Seven countries made explicit requests to the UN outside the named mechanisms (Botswana, Central African Republic, Malawi, Monaco, Singapore, Turkmenistan, Türkiye), including frameworks that are inclusive or development-oriented, Turkmenistan's code for the peaceful use of AI in diplomacy and Türkiye's call to advance a UN convention on AI.

The Global Dialogue on AI Governance was mentioned by 10 countries and supported by 8. Estonia and El Salvador spoke as co-chairs of the first Dialogue session, held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026, and Turkmenistan proposed an expert dialogue in Ashgabat. Chile asked the UN to bring humankind together on AI. Bahrain was more cautious, noting that dialogue can bring positions closer but does not create obligations, while repeating its call for binding rules.

The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI was mentioned by 6 countries and supported by 4 (Barbados, Brazil, Germany, Singapore). Barbados will host the Panel's second in-person meeting in November. Brazil, while supportive, warned of a race “bypassing the United Nations and the scientific panel on artificial intelligence”. The Panel released its preliminary report on 1 July 2026 under a scientific mandate that is policy-relevant but not policy-prescriptive. Verified support for a global AI capacity-building fund came only from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A draft Secretary-General report proposes initial commitments of about $3 billion over four years; no fund has been established.

Much of the activity described in speeches sits alongside or outside the UN. Russia supported China's proposed global AI cooperation organization while welcoming the Dialogue and Panel; Belarus cited that project as evidence that the UN is failing to recognize new trends. The United Kingdom proposed a G20-style approach modelled on the 2008 financial-crisis response, Lithuania promoted the Vilnius Convention, and Japan and India cited the Hiroshima AI Process and India's AI Impact Summit. Norway and Finland called on companies, governments and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier AI models.

AI has become a mainstream General Debate topic: at least two thirds of obtained 2026 addresses referred to it, across every regional group. The dominant demand is for common rules with universal participation, and many speakers name the UN as the venue. Yet a small minority, including the United States, rejects global control schemes, so the Dialogue and Panel operate between broad demand for inclusive rules and open resistance from at least one leading AI state.

Stated demand exceeds current mandates. Calls for binding instruments, pre-release safety testing and a framework convention go beyond the Dialogue's convening role, and military AI concerns fall outside the non-military scope of the Panel and Dialogue. Parallel venues, including the G20, national summits, China's proposed organization and the Vilnius Convention, may compete for relevance unless UN processes show concrete outputs.

For many developing countries the priority is access and capacity, not only risk. With divide and capacity concerns clustered and no funded capacity mechanism in place, progress on the proposed fund is likely to shape perceptions of UN relevance. Because 2025-2026 findings rest on unverified automatic transcripts and 45 addresses remain unresolved, conclusions should be confirmed against official records.

recommendations.action: Frame Secretary-General AI messaging around universal participation in rule-making and practical capacity, and engage sceptical delegations directly rather than presuming consensus.
recommendations.rationale: Inclusive rule-making and UN-role demands are widespread, while four addresses questioned regulation or global approaches.

recommendations.action: Prepare concrete deliverables for the next session, such as shared testing and incident-reporting practices.
recommendations.rationale: Eight countries supported the Dialogue, but Bahrain noted that dialogue creates no obligations, and Germany and Singapore sought common safety standards.

recommendations.action: Advance the proposed Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building with a clear financing path linked to national AI strategy support.
recommendations.rationale: Divide and capacity concerns cluster (20 of 23 capacity-coded addresses also raised the divide), yet verified fund support came from one country.

recommendations.addressee: Independent International Scientific Panel on AI
recommendations.action: Consider language representation, resource footprint and concentration of computing and data in forthcoming assessments.
recommendations.rationale: Egypt, the Bahamas, Malaysia, Botswana and Germany raised these gaps; only four countries voiced explicit Panel support.

recommendations.action: Route military AI and autonomous weapons demands to the appropriate disarmament processes and reference them in Secretary-General messaging.
recommendations.rationale: Thirteen countries raised military AI, which lies outside the non-military Panel and Dialogue.
